title: Trump: Transcript: Trump's 2018 CPAC Speech
description_medium: At the February 23, 2018, Conservative Political Action Conference, Donald Trump celebrated his administration’s first-year record, highlighting judicial confirmations, the tax law and job growth. He praised Neil Gorsuch’s confirmation and said the tax legislation had delivered major cuts. The speech also included an exchange about a protester and criticism of press coverage.
description_long: On February 23, 2018, Donald Trump addressed the Conservative Political Action Conference. The TrumpFile page reproduces a transcript it identifies as originally published by Vox. Trump used the speech to claim credit for judicial confirmations, including Neil Gorsuch, and for the 2017 tax law, which he described as delivering large tax cuts. He also cited 2.7 million jobs and credited congressional allies with helping pass the law, while predicting the absence of Democratic votes could matter in the midterms. The speech mixed policy claims with exchanges about protesters and the press: after an interruption, Trump dismissed it as the act of one person and criticized the attention it might receive. In this address to conservative activists, he presented administration actions as evidence that conservative ideas were being put into practice. This description records the claims and framing in the speech; it does not independently verify the statistics or assess the policies’ effects.
notes: The linked page supplies the full speech transcript; the account summarizes its stated policy claims and event context without treating the speech’s statistics as independently verified.

title: Trump: Benjamin Netanyahu meets with Putin in Moscow, praised by Trump
description_short: Trump: Benjamin Netanyahu meets with Putin in Moscow, praised by Trump
description_medium: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow for about two hours on February 27, 2019. Reports described Iran and Russia’s role in Syria as subjects of the discussion. The meeting came as Netanyahu faced the prospect of an indictment on fraud and bribery allegations in Israel. Donald Trump praised the meeting the next day.
description_long: On February 27, 2019, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow for a meeting reported to have lasted about two hours. The supplied account describes Iran and Russia’s role in Syria as topics, placing the discussion amid regional security tensions. Netanyahu was also awaiting a decision on whether he would face indictment in Israel over fraud and bribery allegations. The following day, President Donald Trump praised the meeting. The record connects the encounter to Trump through that public response; it does not report that he arranged the meeting or took part in it. Nor does the supplied account identify an agreement, announcement or policy change resulting from the talks. The documented episode is therefore a high-level Israeli-Russian meeting, its reported subjects, and Trump’s subsequent praise, rather than evidence of a new U.S. commitment or a changed regional policy.
notes: The supplied synopsis and current draft support the meeting, its reported subjects, Netanyahu’s legal situation and Trump’s next-day praise; no outcome of the meeting is asserted.

title: Trump: FBI tells Bernie Sanders that Russia is boosting him to re-elect Trump (and Trump uses it)
description_short: Trump: FBI tells Bernie Sanders that Russia is boosting him to re-elect Trump (and Trump uses it)
description_medium: In January 2020, the FBI briefed Bernie Sanders or his campaign that Russian activity appeared aimed at boosting his candidacy as a way to help Donald Trump’s reelection. Sanders later confirmed his campaign had received a briefing, though reporting did not name the aides present. Trump subsequently invoked Sanders’s trip to Moscow at a rally, falsely calling it a honeymoon.
description_long: In January 2020, the FBI informed Senator Bernie Sanders or his campaign that Russian activity appeared to be boosting his candidacy as a means of benefiting Donald Trump’s reelection. The intelligence assessment described in the supplied reporting framed the activity as a way to weaken Democrats and ultimately help the incumbent. Sanders later confirmed that his campaign had been briefed, but the linked material does not identify which aides attended. At a Las Vegas rally, Trump asked whether Vladimir Putin would prefer Sanders and said Sanders had “honeymooned in Moscow.” Sanders had visited Russia around the time of his wedding, but the trip was not a honeymoon. Trump’s remark brought a Russia-related talking point into the campaign, although he later said he had not been briefed on the underlying intelligence. The available reporting documents the FBI warning, Sanders’s confirmation and Trump’s public remark; it does not establish that Trump knew the confidential assessment or used it directly. The people receiving the campaign briefing remain unidentified in the supplied sources.
notes: The supplied linked reporting distinguishes the campaign briefing from Trump’s later public remark and does not identify the campaign aides who received the briefing.

title: Trump: More than 10,000 protesters are arrested in just 10 days
description_short: Trump: More than 10,000 protesters are arrested in just 10 days
description_medium: The supplied June 2020 account says more than 10,000 people were arrested at protests across the United States during the ten days after Minneapolis police killed George Floyd on May 25. Demonstrations against police violence spread nationally amid heavy police deployments and city curfews. The packet does not establish a federal order or a direct role for President Trump in the reported arrests.
description_long: The supplied account reports that more than 10,000 people were arrested during protests across the United States in the ten days after Minneapolis police killed George Floyd on May 25, 2020. Demonstrations against police violence spread to cities nationwide, where a heavy police presence and curfews accompanied the protests. The count is attributed to the supplied summary; the packet does not include its underlying methodology or a separate source verifying the total. It also does not establish that President Trump directed local arrests, identify a federal order connected to them, or explain the role of any federal officers in the reported figure. Arrests are not equivalent to convictions, and the summary provides no case outcomes. The account can describe the reported wave of arrests and its protest context, but the title’s placement of the event in a Trump chronology needs a documented link to presidential action or federal policy before it can be treated as a Trump-related event.
notes: The supplied synopsis reports a national arrest count, but the linked TrumpFile page did not provide readable text in the earlier source review. The packet supplies neither the count’s method nor a federal directive or direct Trump role; the event’s Trump connection remains unsupported.
proposed_correction: Attribute the arrest count to a readable source that explains its scope and method, and remove or substantiate the implied Trump connection.

title: Trump: Michael Caputo's HHS adviser: We need to make parents afraid of masks
description_short: Trump: Michael Caputo's HHS adviser: We need to make parents afraid of masks
description_medium: In a September 2020 email to White House adviser Scott Atlas, HHS adviser Paul Alexander proposed another opinion piece about masks and lockdowns and urged messaging that would make parents fear masks. Alexander had been appointed by HHS communications official Michael Caputo. The exchange shows an adviser advocating fear-based public-health messaging during the COVID-19 pandemic.
description_long: In September 2020, Paul Alexander, a health adviser at the Department of Health and Human Services, emailed White House adviser Scott Atlas about publishing another opinion piece on masks and lockdowns. Alexander urged communications that would make parents afraid of masks. The supplied account says this was one of several such emails and describes Alexander as an adviser appointed by HHS communications official Michael Caputo. The message came during the COVID-19 pandemic, when federal officials were publicly debating masking, school precautions and lockdown policy. Its significance lies in the proposed communications strategy: an administration adviser recommended using fear to shape parents’ views of masks, rather than limiting the discussion to evidence and public-health guidance. The materials identify the email’s recipient and subject but do not establish whether Atlas or another official adopted the proposal, whether a specific op-ed was published in response, or what effect the exchange had on policy. The account therefore describes the advocacy in the email without claiming that it changed federal guidance.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
notes: The supplied timeline excerpt identifies Alexander’s email to Atlas and its proposed messaging; no adoption or policy effect is claimed.

title: Trump: Steve Bannon says Trump Admin should murder Dr. Fauci and FBI director
description_short: Trump: Steve Bannon says Trump Admin should murder Dr. Fauci and FBI director
description_medium: On his podcast in November 2020, former Trump strategist Steve Bannon called for the beheading of Dr. Anthony Fauci and FBI Director Christopher Wray, saying their heads should be placed on pikes outside the White House. The remarks were violent rhetoric by a former adviser; the supplied sources do not describe them as an administration plan or action.
description_long: In November 2020, former White House strategist Steve Bannon made violent remarks about Dr. Anthony Fauci and FBI Director Christopher Wray on his “War Room” podcast. He said he would return to the era of Tudor England, put their heads on pikes and place them at the two corners of the White House as a warning to federal bureaucrats. The comments were made publicly after Bannon had left the Trump administration. The supplied reporting documents the statement and the platforms’ response to the episode; it does not establish that Trump or administration officials directed or adopted Bannon’s suggestion. The distinction matters because the event was a former adviser’s call for violence, not evidence that the federal government planned an attack. The remarks targeted the leaders of public-health and federal law-enforcement institutions during a politically charged period. The available account does not establish that either man faced a specific physical threat or that the comments produced a government action.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
notes: The supplied source list and timeline excerpt identify Bannon’s podcast remarks and targets. The account attributes the call to Bannon and does not convert it into an administration order.

title: Trump: Ivanka Trump lies in sworn testimony to DC Attorney General's office
description_short: Trump: Ivanka Trump lies in sworn testimony to DC Attorney General's office
description_medium: Ivanka Trump gave a deposition lasting more than five hours in a D.C. civil lawsuit concerning alleged misuse of donations by the 2017 Presidential Inaugural Committee, including payments to the Trump International Hotel. The Associated Press report confirms her testimony but identifies no false answer or finding of perjury. The title’s accusation is not established by the supplied material.
description_long: In December 2020, Ivanka Trump gave a deposition lasting more than five hours in a civil lawsuit brought by the District of Columbia attorney general over the spending of Donald Trump’s 2017 Presidential Inaugural Committee. The suit alleged that the committee improperly used nonprofit donations, including by paying more than $1 million to the Trump International Hotel in Washington during inauguration week. Ivanka Trump called the inquiry wasteful and said the hotel had been told to charge a fair-market rate. The Associated Press reported that she testified but did not publish an answer shown to be knowingly false or report a perjury charge or finding. The documented event is her testimony in a civil case about alleged inaugural-fund payments; it does not substantiate the title’s claim that she lied under oath. A deposition transcript or an official or judicial finding identifying a specific false answer is needed before that accusation can be stated as fact.
notes: The AP report confirms Ivanka Trump’s deposition and describes the lawsuit’s allegations about inaugural-committee payments, but identifies no knowingly false answer or perjury finding. The title’s central accusation remains unsupported.
proposed_correction: Retitle the entry to describe Ivanka Trump’s deposition in the inaugural-funds lawsuit unless a transcript or official finding substantiates a specific false statement.

title: Trump: 2pm: Pentagon allows disaster at the Capitol, Kevin McCarthy calls Trump
description_short: Trump: 2pm: Pentagon allows disaster at the Capitol, Kevin McCarthy calls Trump
description_medium: On January 6, 2021, as the Capitol was under attack, Capitol Police Chief Steven Sund received reports just before 2 p.m. that rioters had reached the building’s doors. The supplied timeline records Kevin Greeson’s death from a heart attack shortly after 2 p.m.; NBC reporting confirms Kevin McCarthy called Donald Trump during the riot. The title’s Pentagon allegation is not established here.
description_long: On January 6, 2021, supporters of Donald Trump attacked the U.S. Capitol while Congress was meeting to certify the Electoral College results. The supplied timeline says Capitol Police Chief Steven Sund received reports just before 2 p.m. that people outside had reached the doors and were trying to break in. It records that Trump supporter Kevin Greeson was declared dead at 2:05 p.m. after a heart attack. NBC News reported that House Republican leader Kevin McCarthy spoke with Trump during the riot; the supplied material does not establish the call’s exact time or provide a full account of its contents. The title also alleges that the Pentagon “allows disaster,” but the packet does not identify a specific Pentagon order, decision-maker or sequence of requests and responses that would support that charge. The breach interrupted the electoral count and led to deaths and injuries. The described record documents the attack and a call to Trump, while leaving the Pentagon allegation unresolved.
notes: The supplied timeline and NBC report support the Capitol events and McCarthy–Trump call, but do not establish the title’s allegation that the Pentagon allowed the attack or give enough detail to characterize Pentagon decisions.
proposed_correction: Keep the account focused on the documented 2 p.m. events and McCarthy–Trump call, and remove or separately source the Pentagon allegation.

title: Trump: Anti-Corruption Foundation asks Biden to sanction 35 Russians
description_short: Trump: Anti-Corruption Foundation asks Biden to sanction 35 Russians
description_medium: In January 2021, Alexey Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation asked President Joe Biden to sanction 35 Russians it linked to corruption, repression and Navalny’s persecution; eight were placed on a priority list, and seven were already under U.S. sanctions. The request followed Navalny’s return to Russia and detention. The supplied record does not establish a direct Trump connection.
description_long: In January 2021, Alexey Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation asked newly inaugurated President Joe Biden to impose sanctions on 35 Russian figures. A letter reported by CNN placed eight people on a priority shortlist and said seven of the 35 were already subject to U.S. sanctions. The proposed list grouped oligarchs, people accused of suppressing civil and political freedoms, and people the foundation said were involved in persecuting Navalny and his organization. It included billionaire Roman Abramovich and Russian Health Minister Mikhail Murashko; the allegations were attributed to the foundation, and Abramovich’s spokesperson denied them. The appeal came as Navalny was detained after returning to Russia and ahead of a court hearing. The event described is an advocacy request to the Biden administration, not a sanction decision or action by Trump. The packet explains no substantive connection between the request and Trump beyond names that also appear elsewhere in the TrumpFile timeline, so its inclusion in a Trump chronology needs clarification.
notes: CNN reports the foundation’s request and identifies the priority list, but the event is a Biden-era advocacy request. The packet establishes no direct Trump action or material connection beyond cross-references to other timeline entries.
proposed_correction: Retain the account as a report of Navalny’s foundation’s request, and remove the Trump prefix or document a specific Trump-related connection.

title: Trump: Why is Putin's Favorite ‘News' Network Funding the Arizona Recount?
description_short: Trump: Why is Putin's Favorite ‘News' Network Funding the Arizona Recount?
description_medium: During the 2021 Maricopa County audit of the 2020 election, the TrumpFile article reported that One America News Network had started a fundraiser for the review and had been designated a nonpartisan observer. The article criticized that role in light of OANN’s coverage and alleged Russia ties. It does not show that Russian officials funded the audit.
description_long: In April 2021, Cyber Ninjas was conducting a review of the 2020 election in Maricopa County, Arizona. The TrumpFile article reported that One America News Network had launched a fundraiser to support the audit and had also been designated a nonpartisan observer. It cited a New York Times report describing the network’s fundraising effort and argued that OANN’s political alignment and coverage made the observer designation questionable. The article also pointed to U.S. intelligence assessments about Russian efforts to influence American politics and OANN-related content, while characterizing the network as a Russian disinformation outlet. Those characterizations are the article’s argument; they do not establish that the Russian government financed the audit. The supplied materials identify OANN as the outlet and report its fundraising role, but do not state how much it contributed or detail the transfer of money to Cyber Ninjas. The episode raised questions about the audit’s financing and observer standards, without itself establishing foreign-government funding or an audit outcome.
notes: The linked TrumpFile article identifies One America News Network and says it launched a fundraiser and was named a nonpartisan observer. The amount and mechanics of OANN’s contribution are not specified, and the article’s Russia-related characterization is attributed rather than presented as proof of Russian government funding.
